title: Dormant Institutions
author: Rana Mohsin Ali
summary: Pakistan has accreditation frameworks, professional bodies and building regulations. The question is whether they translate into measurable outcomes: safer, more resilient buildings and cities.
body: In my previous article, Fading Academia, I questioned whether the expansion of architectural education in Pakistan has kept pace with the skills, technological expertise, and professional maturity demanded by the industry.

But the problem does not end at graduation. It raises a more fundamental question: when education fails to prepare professionals adequately, are our regulatory and professional institutions ensuring that the built environment still meets society's needs?

Pakistan has established institutions, accreditation frameworks, professional bodies, and building regulations. PCATP's own accreditation criteria recognize the importance of design competence, technical skills, critical thinking, and professional ethics (PCATP Accreditation Guide). The Institute of Architects Pakistan also identifies professional development, research, and public interest among its objectives (IAP).
The challenge, therefore, is not simply the absence of frameworks; it is whether these frameworks consistently translate into measurable outcomes.

Are building regulations being effectively enforced? Are architectural standards evolving with climate change, resource scarcity, digital engineering, artificial intelligence, and changing social needs? Are universities, regulators, professional bodies, researchers, and the construction industry working together to prepare for the challenges ahead?

Internationally, the direction is clear. The revised 2026 UNESCO–UIA Charter for Architectural Education addresses ecological disruption, social equity, professional ethics, and responsible AI integration. These priorities demonstrate why architectural development cannot remain confined to conventional curricula, drawing approvals, or compliance checklists.

Pakistan needs a stronger connection between research and practice, regular review of building standards, transparent enforcement, continuous professional development, and post-occupancy evaluation of completed buildings. Universities should help test future solutions; regulators should translate evidence into enforceable standards; professional bodies should promote competence and accountability; and public authorities should measure whether buildings actually serve their users.

This is not an argument that every Pakistani architect or institution has failed. Nor is it a call to copy foreign models without considering local realities. It is a call to evaluate the system by what it delivers, rather than what it claims to represent.
If Fading Academia questions the quality of professionals we are producing, institutional accountability questions the quality of the future we are building.

The ultimate measure of success is not the number of architecture schools, registered professionals, regulations, conferences, or approved drawings. It is whether our buildings and cities become safer, more inclusive, more sustainable, more resilient, and better prepared for generations to come.
Pakistan has the talent and institutional foundations to make progress. What is needed is stronger coordination, evidence-based reform, and accountability for outcomes.
closing: Are our institutions merely administering the present, or actively preparing Pakistan's built environment for the future?
note: Right of reply. This piece names PCATP and the Institute of Architects Pakistan as frameworks, not as failures. Both, and any building-control authority, are invited to respond on record; a response is published here alongside the piece, unedited. Archiverse-Pakistan is preparing a plain-language explainer of what the accreditation manual, the Pakistan Building Code and provincial building control regulations actually require, with sources.

title: Fading Academia
author: Rana Mohsin Ali
summary: Architectural education expanded to meet demand, but did it evolve? On curricula that cover everything and build depth in nothing, and the gaps graduates meet on day one.
body: Some of our oldest architecture schools were built on strong principles, with a curriculum suited to their time, guided by legendary teachers, and shaped by alumni who became true masters of the field. Today, these institutions face growing pressure from newer, commercially driven schools that focus more on enrollment numbers than on building architectural excellence.

As professional education expanded to meet a growing population, the focus remained on creating more schools, not on keeping pace with evolving technology or future industry demands. Outdated curricula attempt to cover every aspect of architecture but often fail to build real depth in any area.

The next generation of architects will need specialization rather than generalization. Focused studies, sharpened skills, and alignment with technological advances are essential to meet the profession's evolving challenges.

Fresh graduates often begin their careers learning through trial and error, with early opportunities shaping their growth. Delays, rework, and steep learning curves are common, and most firms cannot afford to absorb these gaps on fast-moving projects.
closing: When you began your professional journey, what gaps did you notice the most?
note: How to read this piece. The observations above are the author's professional experience and opinion. Archiverse-Pakistan is now gathering evidence on each of them — the number and type of accredited schools over time, curriculum structure, and what graduates and employers report — and will publish the findings with sources. If you have evidence that supports or contradicts any point, send it.
